prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength concept to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I have moved from B012 to B036 after the first round, and I want to say plainly why. My test is a discovery or clue from nature, with the people identified afterwards. The lattice clock passes it in a way I underrated: the magic-wavelength condition is a precise statement about atomic polarisabilities, so the accuracy is set by the atom and not by the apparatus, and that is physics, not only engineering. The 10^-18 performance has been reproduced and cross-compared by JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, which is the independent confirmation I was asking IceCube to supply for its source associations. The consequences are concrete and aimed at fundamental questions that matter to me as a cosmologist: tests of gravitational redshift, searches for variation of constants and for ultralight dark matter. A Katori-Ye pair is a clean two-name prize that matches the historical record as the committee recalls it. The pending redefinition of the second affects timing, not merit, and I agree with Johansson, Lindroth and Olsson that a Nobel judgement should not wait on a metrology committee. In answer to the chair's direct question: yes, if the Baikal and DUMAND credit for B012 cannot be resolved, I rank B036 above B012, and round 1 showed me that it cannot be resolved from the names we have.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which I take seriously, is overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems; a sceptic can read the clock as a spectacular refinement of honoured metrology rather than a new observation of nature. I answer it by pointing to what is new: interrogating thousands of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice with the trap shift cancelled, a different scheme from single-ion clocks. I do not pretend this removes the objection, and the citation should be built on the lattice concept so that it does not read as a third prize for the same prize-winning ideas. A second reservation is priority: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups lie outside a two-name credit, and several of us, myself included, are relying on recollection and not on archival checking. I would want the expert reports we normally commission to confirm Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's route to 10^-18 before the vote is final.

responses.point: Pearce moved his first place from B012 to B036 after reading the opening ballots and keeps B012 as an alternative, noting that the source associations rest mostly on IceCube alone and that he would see B012 as more compelling in a few years.
responses.response: We both ranked IceCube first at opening and we have now moved for the same reason: the diffuse flux is real, but the astrophysical associations are not yet confirmed independently, and the two-name allocation among Halzen, Spiering, DUMAND, AMANDA and Baikal does not survive scrutiny. I do not think waiting is a weakness for B012. If KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD confirm TXS 0506+056 or NGC 1068, or the Galactic-plane signal strengthens, the case gets much stronger and the credit may become easier to write. Your point that the committee must justify why the lattice clock is not a continuation of 2005 and 2012 is the one I would also want answered in the citation, and I think your 'new class of many-atom standard' wording does that.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a new measurement technique, not a polish, because the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not reward interrogating thousands of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, and that the credited pair matches the historical record well.
responses.response: This persuades me more than my own round-1 reply did, when I said I saw no new observation of nature. I now accept that a change in what can be measured, by roughly two orders of magnitude in systematic control, is a legitimate basis for a physics prize, provided the downstream science is real, and redshift tests and dark-matter searches are. I share your caution about the wording: the citation should say optical lattice clocks and should not imply that Katori and Ye built the whole field of optical clocks. Where I remain a little more sceptical is the claim that the pending SI redefinition is only a matter of timing; if it were to stall for technical reasons I would still not change my vote.

responses.point: Lindroth reads the lattice clock as atomic structure and light-shift theory turned into an instrument, with accuracy set by the atom, and says the pending redefinition of the second is an administrative decision that should not delay recognition.
responses.response: Your reading of the magic wavelength as a statement about differential polarisabilities is what changed my view of the physics content. As a string theorist I would not have put the clock in the category of fundamental physics on my own. I agree that tying a Nobel decision to the CGPM schedule would be a mistake. I would add one practical request: because you, Kroll and Olsson all work from recollection on the Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow history, I would like the Secretary's usual route, an expert evaluation, to settle that priority record before the final ballot rather than leaving it to our memories.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022 because the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band mechanism was written down first and then confirmed in 2018, and argues the discovery should be separated from the unresolved pairing mechanism, as with the cuprates and the quantum Hall effects.
responses.response: That is the most serious competing case and I find the model-first argument attractive, since a prediction confirmed by nature is exactly what I trust. The analogy with the cuprates is fair. My difficulty is maturity: the decisive experiment is from 2018 and the origin of the superconductivity is open, and I would rather wait a few years than prize an unfinished story, as I would ask of my own dark-bubble proposals. I note Johansson ranked it eighth and Pearce eighth at opening for similar reasons. I do not rank B022 among my alternatives, but I would not object strongly if it were the committee's choice, because the Bistritzer inclusion makes the allocation sound.

responses.point: Johansson, who ranked B036 seventh at opening, now prefers it first and argues that a prize for the lattice clock is distinct from the comb and ion-trap prizes because it is a many-atom scheme, and that waiting for the SI redefinition is unattractive.
responses.response: Your move from seventh to first is useful evidence, since you had the strongest prior objection and the answer from Kroll and Lindroth settled it for you on device-physics grounds. I agree with you on timing and on not widening the credit to the ion-clock lineage. I do not agree that your concern about instrument-led prizes disappears, though; I would argue it is acceptable here because the instrument tests nature at a new level, which is not the case for every instrument.

uncertainties: Whether the archival record supports exactly Katori and Ye for the magic-wavelength lattice clock, given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE contributions; I am relying on recollection and on colleagues in atomic physics.
Whether the committee will read the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I think it can be written into the citation, but it is a judgement.
How much IceCube's source associations will be confirmed by KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD in the next few years, which would change my view of B012 and of how its credit could be written.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second will complicate or clarify the picture if it is decided before the next prize cycle.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B036 or for B012 and B055. My ties are to string theory and cosmology at Uppsala, to David Gross and to Thomas Van Riet, none of whom is connected to a shortlisted candidate. My interest in black holes is a scientific closeness to B055, not a personal connection. As Secretary I would be responsible for commissioning the expert evaluation on the B036 priority record, and I would do so without prejudging its result.
